passage:
"Santosh, you asked why I'm so fussy about writing everything in one notebook. Sit. Your Pradeep Chacha will tell you.
In my second year of college, just before Holi, the scholarship office sent me a refund: eight thousand rupees they had overcharged. To me it felt like found money. I bought a watch, treated the whole hostel wing to Holi sweets and took a bus trip to Nashik.
Meanwhile, every morning, I walked forty minutes to class to save six rupees of bus fare, and I skipped the canteen tea to save three. I felt so careful!
By April, when the exam form fee was due, I had nothing. I had been guarding coins with one hand and throwing notes with the other. I had to borrow from your father, and it took me until Diwali to return it."

qa.q: How much was the scholarship refund?
qa.a: Eight thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel careful even while spending the refund so freely?
qa.a: He sorted the refund as found money and the bus fare as real money, so walking to save coins made him feel proud and careful while the notes disappeared.

qa.q: When the refund arrived, what choice could have changed Pradeep's April?
qa.a: He could have counted the refund together with the rest of his money and looked at what was coming, like the exam form fee, before buying the watch or planning the trip.

qa.q: How might Santosh's father have seen the request to borrow?
qa.a: He may have been worried or puzzled that his younger brother had nothing left for the exam form, yet he still chose to help.

grounding: Shows a student spending a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, because separate mental accounts hide his whole picture.

passage:
Every first Sunday my sister Rajni sits at the dining table with one sheet of paper, and I've started watching because it's oddly calming. At the top she writes everything she owns minus everything she owes. Below that, what came in this month and what went out.
She does keep labelled accounts: "Goa trip", "Laptop", "Emergency". But when her office bonus arrived in March, she didn't call it free money. She added it to the sheet like any other rupee, and most of it went into the laptop and emergency pots.
I asked why she bothers with the whole page if the pots are already there.
"The pots are tools, Eshaan," she said, tapping the top line. "This number is the truth."
Last month my own bonus vanished in two weekends. This month I borrowed one of her sheets.

qa.q: What labelled accounts does Rajni keep?
qa.a: "Goa trip", "Laptop" and "Emergency".

qa.q: Why doesn't Rajni treat the March bonus as free money?
qa.a: She seems calm and clear about her money as one whole, so a bonus is just another rupee on the sheet, not a reason to splurge.

qa.q: What makes Rajni's labelled accounts helpful rather than misleading?
qa.a: She uses them only as tools for goals, while the one-page sheet keeps the whole picture, what she owns and owes and what comes and goes, in view.

qa.q: How has watching Rajni affected Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan finds the routine calming and, after a bonus vanished in two weekends, has started using one of her sheets too.

grounding: Shows an earner who treats all money as one pool, tracks what she owns and owes and the monthly flow, and uses labelled accounts only as tools for goals.

passage:
Diwali cleaning day, Saturday
Today Mummy gave me SO many jobs at once. "Jahnavi, fold the clothes, put the diyas on the balcony, water the tulsi, bring the brass lamp from Dadi's room, find the rangoli colours and phone Harish Uncle about lunch."
I said OK and ran. Then I stood in the hall and could only remember the diyas. I put them out and came back.
Mummy sighed. "And the rest?" I felt so stupid 😔
Then Harish Uncle turned up anyway. "Too many at once, na? Let's do three." He wrote 1, 2, 3 on my palm with a pen: clothes, tulsi, lamp. I did all three! Then three more.
Tomorrow I'm making my own list.

qa.q: What did Harish Uncle write on Jahnavi's palm?
qa.a: He wrote 1, 2, 3 on the palm: clothes, tulsi, lamp.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Mummy asked "And the rest?"
qa.a: Jahnavi felt stupid and sad, because only the diyas had stayed in memory out of the whole long list 😔

qa.q: What could Mummy try the next time she has lots of jobs for Jahnavi?
qa.a: She could give two or three jobs at a time, or write them down the way Harish Uncle did, so they fit in Jahnavi's head.

qa.q: What might Mummy have been thinking when she sighed?
qa.a: Mummy was probably tired and rushed on cleaning day, and may not have noticed how many jobs she had given at once.

grounding: Shows a child forgetting most of a long list of instructions and managing well once the jobs come in short steps.

passage:
Monday, first week of the summer holidays. Saurabh sat with his biology notes, a song with loud lyrics in one ear and his phone buzzing with the cricket group every minute. He read the page on photosynthesis three times.
Wednesday. Damini, his sister, quizzed him at dinner. "Where does the light reaction happen?" Saurabh opened his mouth. Nothing. "I read it three times!" he groaned, cheeks hot. "It just slid off."
Saturday. As an experiment, Damini took his phone to her room and put on quiet music without words. Saurabh read the page once, slowly, then drew the diagram from memory. At dinner he answered all five of her questions and looked almost suspicious about it.

qa.q: How many times did Saurabh read the page on Monday?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when he couldn't answer Damini's question?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and embarrassed, groaning with hot cheeks, because he had read it three times and it still slid off.

qa.q: What small change helped Saurabh, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone in Damini's room and switching to music without words, because his attention was no longer split and the page could stick.

qa.q: What might Damini have noticed that Saurabh didn't?
qa.a: Damini seemed to notice that the buzzing phone and the lyrics were crowding his mind, which is why she suggested the experiment.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose studying does not stick while a phone buzzes and lyrics play, because attention and memory are overloaded.

passage:
The campus bookshop was packed during winter fest week, and Yash was working the evening till between mock exams. His phone kept lighting up with messages from home about Nanaji's hospital tests.
He gave a customer change for two hundred instead of five hundred. He shelved the chemistry guides under history. At seven he noticed he had written yesterday's date on the delivery sheet. Twice.
"Yash, the stapler is in your hand," Hafsa said gently, as he searched the drawer for it.
He laughed, but it came out shaky. "My head's like a browser with forty tabs open."
Hafsa, the shift supervisor, pulled out a stool. "Sit for five minutes. Drink some water. Then just the till, nothing else, until eight."
He sat, pressing his palms against his eyes. The noise of the fest drifted in from the lawn.

qa.q: What was Yash searching the drawer for?
qa.a: The stapler, which was in his hand.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling during his shift, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and anxious, shown by the careless mistakes, the shaky laugh and his line about a browser with forty tabs open.

qa.q: How did Hafsa lighten Yash's load?
qa.a: She gave him a short break with water and then narrowed his job to just the till until eight.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Yash's mistakes?
qa.a: She seems to see them as signs of an overloaded mind rather than carelessness, since she responds gently instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a student juggling exams, work and worry who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy.

passage:
By Tuesday afternoon the grant report for the community library was due in two days, and the shared office buzzed with calls. Farhan, at the next desk, had eleven tabs open and kept jumping between emails.
Shalini's screen showed one document. Her phone lay face down, set to let through only calls from her manager. A sticky note on the monitor listed the report in five steps: numbers, stories, photos, budget table, summary. Two were crossed out.
Every hour she stood, filled her water bottle and looked out of the window for a few minutes. When a thought popped up, like booking a cab for Friday, she scribbled it on a pad and went back to the stories.
Farhan leaned over. "How are you so calm?"
"I'm not holding it all in my head," she said. "Paper holds it for me."

qa.q: How many steps were on Shalini's sticky note?
qa.a: Five: numbers, stories, photos, budget table and summary.

qa.q: Why does Shalini feel calm with the report due in two days?
qa.a: The steps, stray thoughts and notifications are all handled outside her head, so she feels steady enough to focus on one section at a time.

qa.q: What could Farhan copy from Shalini first?
qa.a: He could write the job down as a few steps and close most of the eleven tabs, so he works on one thing at a time.

qa.q: What is it like for Farhan sitting next to Shalini?
qa.a: Farhan feels scattered, jumping between eleven tabs and emails, and is curious and a little envious of how calm she seems.

grounding: Shows a worker who writes things down, breaks a big job into steps, silences needless notifications and takes breaks so she can focus on what matters.

passage:
Yusuf's first week on our support team, I watched him drown. On Monday the manager walked him through the ticket system, the refund rules, forty-two ready-made replies and the escalation chart in one ninety-minute session. By Wednesday he was answering customers with the wrong template and apologising to everyone.
I remembered my own first week, crying in the washroom over that same chart.
So on Thursday I closed the chart. "Today, just one thing: password resets," I told him. I showed him three real examples, taped a six-line checklist to his monitor, and let him do ten while I sat beside him. Friday was delivery complaints. The week after, refunds.
By the end of the month he was the one explaining password resets to the next new joiner. I'm Gurleen, and that checklist tape is still in my drawer.

qa.q: What was the one thing Yusuf learned on Thursday?
qa.a: Password resets.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel while watching Yusuf struggle, and why?
qa.a: Gurleen felt a pang of sympathy, remembering crying in the washroom over the same chart in that first week.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen's steps could any trainer use?
qa.a: Teaching one topic a day, showing a few real examples, giving a short checklist and letting the newcomer practise with support nearby.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt by Wednesday of his first week?
qa.a: He probably felt overwhelmed and embarrassed, using the wrong templates and apologising to everyone after too much information at once.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague who sees a new hire overloaded and teaches in small stages with examples, a checklist and time to practise.

passage:
In the Jaipur flat, Saurabh sat on the rug stacking red cups into a wobbly tower, tongue poking out.
"Saurabh! Bath time!" Mumma called from the hallway. Nothing.
"Saurabh!" Louder. Still nothing. The tower grew.
His big brother Harsha grumbled, "He's ignoring you on purpose."
Mumma knelt beside Saurabh and touched his shoulder. He looked up, startled, then beamed and held out a cup. "Mumma, see!"

qa.q: What was Saurabh stacking?
qa.a: Red cups, into a wobbly tower.

qa.q: Why didn't Saurabh answer when Mumma called?
qa.a: He was so absorbed in the tower that he didn't hear his name; when she touched him he looked startled, then happy to share it.

qa.q: What worked to get Saurabh's attention?
qa.a: Kneeling beside him and touching his shoulder worked, because it reached him inside his focus.

qa.q: Why might Harsha react differently from Mumma?
qa.a: Harsha thinks Saurabh is ignoring her on purpose, while Mumma treats it as normal absorption and goes to him.

grounding: Shows a toddler so absorbed in a toy that he does not hear his name, a normal limit rather than defiance.

passage:
At the Baisakhi fair in the village, a puppet show began under the neem tree. Simran sat in the front row, mouth open, as the wooden king chased the wooden thief round and round.
During the chase, Ayesha Aunty walked right past the stage in a bright yellow dupatta, carrying a basket of oranges, and waved at Simran.
Simran didn't blink.
Afterwards Ayesha Aunty laughed. "I waved at you!"
"You didn't come," Simran said, puzzled. "I was watching the king the whole time."

qa.q: What was Ayesha Aunty carrying when she walked past the stage?
qa.a: A basket of oranges.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Ayesha Aunty said she had waved?
qa.a: Simran felt puzzled, because the chase held all her attention and the aunty in yellow never seemed to appear.

qa.q: How could a grown-up get Simran's attention during a show?
qa.a: They could wait for a pause, or kneel beside her and touch her arm, since waving from a distance won't reach her while she is absorbed.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha Aunty when Simran doesn't wave back?
qa.a: Ayesha Aunty finds it funny rather than rude, and laughs about it afterwards.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so focused on a puppet show that a person walking past vanishes from her view.

passage:
On the last day before the Holi holidays, Mehak Didi brought her laptop to the little science club at the kasba school. "Watch the players in white shirts. Count how many times they pass the ball. Only white!"
Mohit leaned in, lips moving. Nine, ten, eleven. He ignored the black shirts completely. Fifteen, sixteen.
"Sixteen!" he shouted when it ended.
"Correct," said Mehak Didi. "And did anyone see the bear?"
"What bear?"
She played it again. Halfway through, a person in a fluffy bear costume strolled right through the middle of the players, waved, and walked off.
Mohit's jaw dropped. "That was NOT there before!"
"It was," Mehak Didi said, smiling. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention was busy."

qa.q: Which players did Mehak Didi ask the club to watch?
qa.a: The players in white shirts.

qa.q: What does Mohit's "That was NOT there before!" suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt astonished and a bit disbelieving, since he was sure he had watched everything closely while counting.

qa.q: What could Mohit do when something important might be missed?
qa.a: He could remember that focusing hard on one task can hide other things, and take a second look or ask others what they noticed.

qa.q: Why might Mehak Didi enjoy showing the video twice?
qa.a: She knows the surprise will help the club remember that attention, not the eyes alone, decides what they see.

grounding: Shows a child so busy counting passes that a costumed figure walking through the video goes unseen.
